title: How change control and configuration management fit together
blurb: Explain how change control and configuration management depend on each other, and what breaks if one is missing.
question: A hospital app project approves a change to add text-message reminders, but developers then build it from an out-of-date screen design. Which discipline worked, which failed, and why does a project need both?

teach.body: Change control decides WHETHER a change to the baseline is made. Configuration management controls and records WHAT the items are and which version is current. Put together, only authorised changes are implemented, and the status of every item is always known. Neither works properly alone: they depend on each other.

teach.caption: Different activities, one goal: the scope changes only in an authorised, recorded way.

teach.body: Northgate Hospital is building a patient app. Its screen specification, SMS interface and privacy notice are all configuration items with versions. Clinicians raise CR-07: add appointment reminders by text. To assess it, the team first checks the configuration records to see exactly which items CR-07 would touch. That is configuration management feeding change control.

steps.label: Evaluate the change
steps.sub: Impact on scope, time, cost, quality and risk

steps.label: Update the records
steps.sub: v3.0 shown as current, citing CR-07; v2.0 withdrawn

teach.caption: Steps 1, 4 and 5 are configuration management; steps 2 and 3 are change control.

teach.body: Change control needs configuration management: without accurate records you cannot tell what a change would affect, so impact assessment is guesswork. Configuration management needs change control: it should only update an item when a change has been authorised. An approved change updates the configuration and its records, so the next request is judged against the true current state.

teach.h: What breaks if one is missing
teach.caption: Each half on its own leaves a gap the other is designed to fill.

items.label: Baseline set at v1.0
items.sub: Config mgmt: every item identified and labelled

items.label: CR-07 raised and assessed
items.sub: Both: the records show which items it affects

items.label: CR-07 approved; items updated
items.sub: Change control decides; config mgmt moves items to new versions

items.label: CR-09 rejected
items.sub: Change control: no item changes; decision logged

items.label: Final audit
items.sub: Config mgmt: records checked against the delivered app

teach.caption: Change control acts when a request arrives. Configuration management runs continuously.
Each approved change produces a new, recorded version that the next request is judged against.

teach.text: Classic swap: configuration management does NOT approve or reject changes, and change control does NOT keep the version history. If an option gives the approval job to configuration management, or the record-keeping job to change control, it is wrong.

items: Change control decides whether a change to the baseline is made.
Configuration management controls and records what the items are and which version is current.
Configuration records support the impact assessment of a change request.
An approved change updates the configuration and its records: only authorised changes, every status known.

summary: You can now explain how change control and configuration management depend on each other: records feed the assessment, decisions drive the updates. You can also say what goes wrong when either one is missing.

A.q: Complete the statement: change control decides whether a change is made, while configuration management…
options: sets the budget available for each change
records the items and their current versions
approves the change on the sponsor's behalf
measures the benefits the change delivers
A.why: Configuration management controls and records what the items are and which version is current.

whyNot.0: Budgets are set through cost management and governance, not configuration management.
whyNot.2: Approval is part of change control and sits with the sponsor or appropriate authority.

A.q: The Northgate team must assess CR-07. Which configuration management output helps them most?
options: The benefits realisation plan
The stakeholder engagement plan
The configuration records
The lessons learned log
A.why: Configuration records show which items, at which versions, the change would affect: the basis of a sound impact assessment.

whyNot.0: The benefits plan helps judge value but is not a configuration management output.
whyNot.1: The engagement plan supports communication, not the identification of affected items.
whyNot.3: The lessons log captures learning from past work, not the current state of items.

A.q: CR-07 has been approved and built. What should the configuration records now show?
options: The original version as still current
Only the name of the person who asked
The approved budget for the change
The new version as current, with history
A.why: An approved change updates the configuration and its records: the new version is current and the history is kept.

whyNot.0: Leaving the old version marked current is exactly the error configuration management prevents.
whyNot.1: The requester is recorded in the change log, but the records must show the new item version.
whyNot.2: Budget changes go in the plans and cost records, not the item's configuration status.

B.q: Which is the most likely result of change control operating without configuration management?
options: No one could raise a change request
Approved changes may not be traceable
The sponsor could not approve changes
The project would have no business case
B.why: Without configuration management, approved changes may be made without the resulting versions being recorded, so they cannot be traced.

whyNot.0: Requests can still be raised; the gap is in recording what changes as a result.
whyNot.2: The approval route is part of change control, which still exists here.
whyNot.3: The business case is unaffected by whether configuration management exists.

B.q: Which is the most likely result of configuration management operating without change control?
options: Unauthorised changes are recorded neatly
Items can no longer be given unique labels
Version history can no longer be recorded
Status reports can no longer be produced
B.why: With no authorisation step, changes still happen and are faithfully recorded, but nobody approved them: well-documented scope creep.

whyNot.1: Labelling items is configuration management, which is still operating.
whyNot.2: Recording version history is configuration management, which is still operating.
whyNot.3: Status reporting is configuration management, which is still operating.

B.q: Which statement about the timing of the two disciplines is correct?
options: Both operate only during project closure
Change control runs before any baseline
Configuration management is continuous
Configuration management runs once only
B.why: Configuration management runs throughout the project to keep records current; change control acts whenever a change is requested.

whyNot.0: Both are needed throughout delivery, not just at closure.
whyNot.1: Change control protects an approved baseline, so it applies once a baseline exists.
whyNot.3: Item records must be kept current all the time, not set once and left.

C.q: Northgate's sponsor approves CR-07, but developers build it from an out-of-date screen design. Where did control break down?
options: In change control: the decision was wrong
In risk management: no risk was raised
In benefits management: no profile existed
In configuration management: wrong version
C.why: The change was properly authorised, so change control worked. Building from the wrong version is a configuration management failure.

whyNot.0: The decision followed the process; the failure happened after it.
whyNot.1: A missing risk entry does not explain why the wrong version was used.
whyNot.2: Benefits planning has nothing to do with which design version was built.

C.q: Which TWO statements are correct? 1. Configuration records support the impact assessment of a change. 2. Configuration management approves changes to the baseline. 3. An approved change updates the configuration and its records. 4. Change control keeps each item's version history.
options: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
C.why: Records feed the assessment (1) and approved changes update the configuration and records (3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is false: approval belongs to change control.
whyNot.1: Both are false: they swap the two disciplines' jobs.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is false: version history is kept by configuration management.

C.q: An auditor asks Northgate's PM to prove that every change made to the app was authorised. What evidence shows this best?
options: The change log matched to version records
The latest risk register and issue log
The team's weekly highlight reports
The original business case document
C.why: Each new version in the configuration records cites an approved request in the change log, proving every change was authorised.

whyNot.1: Risks and issues show threats and problems, not which changes were approved and built.
whyNot.2: Highlight reports summarise progress; they do not trace each version to an approval.
whyNot.3: The business case justifies the project; it says nothing about later changes.

reteach.title: Think of planning a wedding
reteach.question: Aunt Jo asks to bring three extra guests. Who decides, and how does everyone end up with the right seating plan?

blocks.h: The couple and the seating plan
blocks.body: The seating plan is the configuration item: version 4 is the one the venue holds. Aunt Jo's request is a change request. The couple first look at plan v4 to see the knock-on effect: a new table, more meals, a tighter room. Then they decide yes. Plan v5 goes to the venue and v4 is withdrawn. Deciding is change control; keeping one current plan is configuration management.

steps.label: Request arrives
steps.sub: Aunt Jo asks for three more places

steps.label: Check plan v4
steps.sub: What would it affect? Tables, meals, space

blocks.text: If the venue kept two different plans, the decision would be wasted. If the planner updated the plan without asking the couple, the records would be neat but the change unauthorised. You need both halves.

explain.body: Change control's part in the partnership is the decision: should this change to the baseline be made? It captures the request, weighs up the impact and gets a decision from the right authority.

test.q: In the partnership, which question does change control answer?
options: Which version is current?
Where is the item stored?
Should this change be made?
Who owns this document?
test.why: Change control decides whether a proposed change to the baseline goes ahead.

whyNot.0: The current version is shown by configuration management records.
whyNot.1: Where items are held is set up under configuration management.
whyNot.3: Item ownership is recorded as part of configuration management.

explain.body: Configuration management's part is the record: what each item is, which version is current and how it got there. It means everyone builds from the right version and the status of every item is known.

test.q: In the partnership, which question does configuration management answer?
options: Is the change worth doing?
Which version is current?
Who should fund the change?
Should the sponsor approve?
test.why: Configuration management records what the items are and which version is current.

whyNot.0: Whether a change is worthwhile is judged through change control.
whyNot.2: Funding comes from the change decision and budget management, not configuration records.
whyNot.3: Approval is change control's decision, not configuration management's.

explain.body: Before a change can be judged, you need to know what it touches. The configuration records list the affected items, their versions and the items linked to them, so the impact assessment is based on facts, not guesswork.

steps.label: Impact assessment
steps.sub: What CR-07 would change, and the knock-on

test.q: Why are configuration records useful when a change request is being assessed?
options: They decide the change for the sponsor
They remove the need for an impact study
They replace the project's change log
They show what the change would affect
test.why: The records identify the items, and their versions, that the change would touch.

whyNot.0: Records inform the decision; the sponsor or appropriate authority makes it.
whyNot.1: Records support the impact assessment; they do not replace it.
whyNot.2: The change log tracks requests and decisions; configuration records track items. Both are needed.

explain.body: When a change is approved, configuration management updates the affected items and their records. The new version becomes current, the old one is withdrawn but kept in the history, and the record cites the change request.

steps.label: Old version withdrawn
steps.sub: Kept in the history, no longer used

test.q: Once a change is approved and implemented, what happens to the previous version of the item?
options: It is withdrawn but kept in the history
It stays in use alongside the new one
It is deleted so nobody can find it
It becomes the new project baseline
test.why: The old version is withdrawn from use but kept in the history, so every change stays traceable.

whyNot.1: Two versions in use at once is exactly the confusion configuration management prevents.
whyNot.2: Deleting it would destroy the history needed for traceability.
whyNot.3: The new, approved version forms the updated baseline, not the old one.
